difficultyReason: The stimulus contains an intermediate conclusion marked with 'thus' that tempts test-takers to select it as the main point. The actual main conclusion appears at the end without an explicit marker, requiring careful tracking of argument structure.
stimulus: Antibiotic resistance has accelerated sharply over the past two decades. Hospitals that restrict antibiotic prescriptions to cases where bacterial infection is confirmed show significantly lower rates of resistant strains than hospitals with more permissive prescription policies. Thus, overprescription of antibiotics is a leading driver of resistance. Physicians who continue to prescribe antibiotics for viral illnesses are therefore contributing to a public health crisis that will eventually render many life-saving drugs ineffective.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotic resistance has increased sharply over the past two decades.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Overprescription of antibiotics is a leading driver of antibiotic resistance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hospitals with restrictive prescription policies have lower rates of resistant bacterial strains.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Physicians who prescribe antibiotics for viral illnesses are contributing to a public health crisis that will eventually render many life-saving drugs ineffective.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Antibiotic resistance will eventually make all current medications useless if prescribing practices do not improve worldwide.

explanations.correct: The final sentence, signaled by 'therefore,' is the argument's main conclusion. It identifies the specific agents responsible (physicians prescribing for viral illnesses) and names the ultimate consequence (rendering life-saving drugs ineffective). Every prior claim — the trend data, the hospital comparison, and the intermediate conclusion about overprescription — serves as support for this claim.
explanations.A: Premise trap. This is background context that supports the intermediate conclusion; it is not the claim the argument is building toward.
explanations.B: Intermediate-conclusion trap. This sentence is marked with 'thus' and serves as a stepping stone to the final 'therefore' claim. It is a subsidiary conclusion, not the main point.
explanations.C: Premise trap. The hospital data is offered as evidence for the intermediate conclusion about overprescription, not as the argument's destination.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the 'therefore' claim at the end of the argument, toward which all other statements point.
explanations.E: Overstatement trap. The stimulus says many life-saving drugs may become ineffective; it does not claim all current medications will become useless, nor does it assert a worldwide prescribing-improvement condition.

difficultyReason: The stimulus opens with the main conclusion before providing layered support, including an intermediate conclusion. Test-takers who read the argument linearly may mistake the intermediate claim or the final supporting sentence for the main point.
stimulus: The city council should reject the proposed downtown parking garage. Surveys show that cities which invest in parking infrastructure experience a corresponding increase in automobile traffic, not a reduction in congestion as proponents claim. Furthermore, increased automobile traffic generates higher carbon emissions, thus worsening the city's already poor air quality. The council has repeatedly committed to improving air quality as a top priority, and approving this garage would directly contradict that commitment.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Building parking garages in city centers causes automobile traffic to increase rather than decrease.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The city council has a prior commitment to improving air quality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased automobile traffic worsens air quality by generating higher carbon emissions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The proposed parking garage will worsen the city's air quality and should therefore be rejected by the city council.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The city council should reject the proposed downtown parking garage.

explanations.correct: The opening sentence states the main conclusion directly: the council should reject the garage. All subsequent claims — the traffic data, the air quality chain, and the council's prior commitment — are marshaled as support for that recommendation. Choice E faithfully paraphrases this conclusion.
explanations.A: Premise trap. The survey finding about parking infrastructure and traffic is offered as evidence; it is not what the argument is ultimately trying to establish.
explanations.B: Premise trap. The council's commitment to air quality is a supporting fact used to show the garage would contradict council policy, not the conclusion itself.
explanations.C: Intermediate-conclusion trap. This is the 'thus'-marked subsidiary claim linking traffic to air quality; it supports the main point but is not itself the main point.
explanations.D: Mis-scoped trap. While accurate in substance, this choice conflates the intermediate conclusion (worsens air quality) with the main recommendation in a way that makes air quality the stated reason rather than presenting the recommendation on its own terms. Choice E more accurately and cleanly paraphrases the opening main conclusion.
explanations.E: Correct. This directly paraphrases the argument's opening sentence, which is the claim all supporting sentences are designed to establish.

difficultyReason: The argument opens with an opposing view that students may misread as the conclusion. The author's actual conclusion appears at the end and is distinguished by a first-person rebuttal structure, requiring attention to the opposing-view/author's-view distinction.
stimulus: Some economists argue that free trade agreements invariably benefit all participating nations by lowering consumer prices and expanding markets. This view overlooks a critical asymmetry: nations with robust labor protections bear higher production costs than those without such protections, and thus cannot compete on equal terms. Companies therefore relocate production to lower-protection nations, hollowing out the industrial base of high-protection countries. Free trade agreements, as currently structured, systematically disadvantage nations that maintain strong labor standards.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Free trade agreements lower consumer prices and expand markets for all participating nations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nations with strong labor protections face higher production costs than nations without such protections.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Companies relocate production to nations with lower labor-protection standards when free trade agreements are in place.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Free trade agreements, as currently structured, systematically disadvantage nations that maintain strong labor standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Free trade agreements should be renegotiated to eliminate the cost asymmetries between high- and low-protection nations.

explanations.correct: The final sentence is the author's main conclusion, the claim the entire argument is building toward. The preceding sentences rebut the opposing economist view and provide the causal chain (cost asymmetry → relocation → industrial hollowing) that supports this conclusion.
explanations.A: Opposing-view misread trap. This is the view the author attributes to 'some economists' and then argues against. It is the position being rebutted, not the author's conclusion.
explanations.B: Premise trap. The cost asymmetry between high- and low-protection nations is a supporting fact in the causal chain, not the conclusion.
explanations.C: Intermediate-conclusion trap. The 'therefore' in the prior sentence signals this as a subsidiary conclusion that in turn supports the final claim about systematic disadvantage.
explanations.D: Correct. This accurately paraphrases the final sentence, which is the author's overarching claim that all the argument's evidence is designed to support.
explanations.E: Overstatement trap. The author does not recommend renegotiation; the argument only establishes that current agreements disadvantage high-standards nations. Introducing a policy prescription goes beyond what the stimulus concludes.

difficultyReason: The argument has a clear intermediate conclusion mid-stimulus that carries its own explicit 'hence' marker. The main conclusion appears at the end without a marker, requiring students to distinguish between the subsidiary and main claims.
stimulus: Linguists have documented that children raised in bilingual households acquire both languages without apparent cognitive penalty and often outperform monolingual peers on tasks requiring mental flexibility. The ability to switch between two grammatical systems exercises executive control mechanisms, hence strengthening general cognitive flexibility. Parents who expose their children to a second language from birth are therefore giving those children a measurable cognitive advantage that extends well beyond language itself.
questionStem: The main point of the argument is that

choices.label: A
choices.text: children raised in bilingual households outperform monolingual children on all cognitive tasks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: switching between two grammatical systems exercises executive control mechanisms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: parents who raise their children bilingually from birth provide them with a cognitive advantage extending beyond language.

choices.label: D
choices.text: bilingualism strengthens cognitive flexibility by exercising executive control mechanisms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: linguists have established that bilingual children acquire both languages without cognitive penalty.

explanations.correct: The final sentence, marked by 'therefore,' is the main conclusion. It identifies the relevant agents (parents who expose children to a second language from birth) and the specific benefit (a measurable cognitive advantage extending beyond language). All prior claims — the research data and the intermediate conclusion about flexibility — support this claim.
explanations.A: Overstatement trap. The stimulus says bilingual children often outperform monolinguals on tasks requiring mental flexibility, not on all cognitive tasks.
explanations.B: Premise trap. This is a factual claim in the causal chain offered as support for the intermediate conclusion about flexibility.
explanations.C: Correct. This accurately paraphrases the 'therefore' sentence at the argument's end.
explanations.D: Intermediate-conclusion trap. This paraphrases the 'hence' sentence, which is a subsidiary conclusion. It supports the main conclusion but is not itself the main point.
explanations.E: Premise trap. The linguists' findings are background evidence cited to support the argument, not its conclusion.

difficultyReason: The argument structure places the main conclusion first, with both an intermediate conclusion and multiple premises following. One distractor paraphrases the intermediate conclusion, and another restates background context, requiring careful identification of what the argument ultimately seeks to establish.
stimulus: Contemporary art museums should not rely primarily on blockbuster exhibitions to attract visitors. It is true that such exhibitions draw large crowds and generate significant short-term revenue. However, blockbuster exhibitions crowd out smaller, experimental shows, thus depriving emerging artists of exhibition opportunities. Moreover, institutions that chase crowd-pleasing spectacles gradually lose the curatorial independence that makes them intellectually relevant. A museum that sacrifices curatorial integrity for attendance figures ultimately undermines its own cultural mission.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockbuster exhibitions generate significant short-term revenue and draw large crowds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockbuster exhibitions deprive emerging artists of exhibition opportunities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Art museums that sacrifice curatorial integrity for attendance figures ultimately undermine their cultural mission.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Contemporary art museums should not rely primarily on blockbuster exhibitions to attract visitors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Institutions that pursue crowd-pleasing spectacles lose their curatorial independence entirely.

explanations.correct: The opening sentence is the main conclusion, and every subsequent claim — the concession about revenue, the loss of opportunities for emerging artists, the decline of curatorial independence, and the final summarizing sentence — all serve to support it. Choice D paraphrases the opening claim faithfully.
explanations.A: Premise trap. This is the concession acknowledged in 'It is true that…'; it is a supporting observation, not the claim the argument is trying to establish.
explanations.B: Intermediate-conclusion trap. The 'thus' before 'depriving emerging artists' marks this as a subsidiary conclusion that supports the main point but is not itself the main point.
explanations.C: Mis-scoped / supporting-summary trap. The final sentence is a general restatement that functions as a supporting summary for the specific recommendation in the opening sentence. The argument's actionable conclusion concerns museums relying primarily on blockbusters, not a general claim about sacrificing integrity.
explanations.D: Correct. This faithfully paraphrases the first sentence, which is the recommendation that all remaining claims are marshaled to support.
explanations.E: Overstatement trap. The argument says museums 'gradually lose' curatorial independence, not that they lose it 'entirely.'

difficultyReason: The argument involves a legal policy context with an intermediate conclusion clearly marked by 'so.' A distractor paraphrases only the intermediate conclusion, and another mirrors the conceded opposing view. The main conclusion appears at the end.
stimulus: Some legal scholars contend that mandatory minimum sentencing laws reduce crime by ensuring consistent, deterrent punishments. Yet jurisdictions that have repealed mandatory minimums have not experienced corresponding increases in violent crime rates. Judges given discretion to tailor sentences to individual circumstances produce outcomes that correctional experts consider more rehabilitative, so mandatory minimums reduce neither recidivism nor crime in practice. Legislatures would therefore better serve public safety by replacing mandatory minimums with structured sentencing guidelines that preserve judicial discretion.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentencing laws reduce crime by ensuring consistent deterrent punishments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jurisdictions that repealed mandatory minimums have not seen increases in violent crime rates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentencing laws reduce neither recidivism nor crime in practice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Judges given discretion produce more rehabilitative sentencing outcomes than mandatory minimums allow.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Legislatures would better serve public safety by replacing mandatory minimums with structured sentencing guidelines that preserve judicial discretion.

explanations.correct: The final sentence, marked by 'therefore,' is the main conclusion: a specific legislative recommendation. The argument's entire evidentiary structure — the crime-rate data, the rehabilitative outcomes finding, and the intermediate conclusion about recidivism — all build toward this policy prescription.
explanations.A: Opposing-view misread trap. This is the view attributed to 'some legal scholars' that the argument then rebuts. It is the position being argued against, not the author's conclusion.
explanations.B: Premise trap. The crime-rate data from jurisdictions that repealed mandatory minimums is evidence supporting the intermediate conclusion; it is not the conclusion itself.
explanations.C: Intermediate-conclusion trap. The 'so' marker identifies this as a subsidiary conclusion that supports the final 'therefore' recommendation but is not itself the main point.
explanations.D: Premise trap. The rehabilitative outcomes finding is a supporting fact used in conjunction with other evidence to reach the intermediate conclusion about recidivism.
explanations.E: Correct. This accurately paraphrases the 'therefore' sentence that concludes the argument with a specific policy recommendation.

difficultyReason: The stimulus addresses an environmental science topic and buries the intermediate conclusion in the middle with an explicit 'thus.' The main conclusion appears last with 'it follows that,' but one distractor paraphrases the intermediate conclusion, and another overstates the scope.
stimulus: Old-growth forests store carbon at a rate far exceeding that of replanted forests because their complex biomass — including deadwood, deep root systems, and layered understory — accumulates carbon over centuries. Replanted forests, by contrast, release significant carbon during the harvesting and replanting process, thus yielding a net carbon deficit for several decades after logging. Old-growth deforestation therefore accelerates atmospheric carbon accumulation. It follows that preserving existing old-growth forests is a more effective near-term climate strategy than any program of compensatory reforestation.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Old-growth forests store carbon at a far higher rate than replanted forests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Replanted forests yield a net carbon deficit for several decades after logging.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Old-growth deforestation accelerates the accumulation of carbon in the atmosphere.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preserving existing old-growth forests is a more effective near-term climate strategy than any compensatory reforestation program.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All deforestation programs should be halted immediately to prevent irreversible climate damage.

explanations.correct: The final sentence, introduced by 'it follows that,' is the main conclusion. It makes the specific comparative claim — old-growth preservation beats compensatory reforestation as a near-term climate strategy — that the entire argument's evidence and subsidiary conclusions are designed to establish.
explanations.A: Premise trap. The comparison of carbon-storage rates is background evidence supporting the intermediate conclusion; it is not itself the argument's destination.
explanations.B: Intermediate-conclusion trap. The 'thus' marker identifies the net-carbon-deficit claim as a subsidiary conclusion. It supports the penultimate sentence and ultimately the main conclusion, but it is not the main point.
explanations.C: Mis-scoped intermediate-conclusion trap. 'Old-growth deforestation accelerates atmospheric carbon accumulation' is the second intermediate conclusion, marked by 'therefore.' It is a stepping stone to the final 'it follows that' claim, not the main point.
explanations.D: Correct. This faithfully paraphrases the final 'it follows that' sentence, which is the argument's main conclusion.
explanations.E: Overstatement trap. The argument makes a near-term comparative claim about old-growth preservation versus reforestation; it does not advocate halting all deforestation programs or predict irreversible damage.

difficultyReason: The argument is from the domain of technology ethics. The main conclusion is stated first, but two intermediate conclusions follow and each uses its own support, making it tempting to select one of those subsidiary claims as the main point.
stimulus: Technology companies should be required to disclose the training data used to develop their artificial intelligence systems. Without such disclosure, independent researchers cannot identify whether training datasets contain systematic biases, so claims of algorithmic fairness remain unverifiable. Furthermore, undisclosed training data makes it impossible for affected individuals to challenge decisions made about them by those systems, thus denying them meaningful recourse. Transparency in AI development is the foundation of both accountability and trust.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Without disclosure of training data, claims of algorithmic fairness cannot be independently verified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Technology companies should be required to disclose the training data used to build their AI systems.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Undisclosed training data prevents affected individuals from challenging decisions AI systems make about them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transparency in AI development is necessary for both accountability and trust.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Artificial intelligence systems that rely on biased training data will inevitably produce unfair outcomes.

explanations.correct: The opening sentence is the main conclusion: a specific regulatory recommendation that technology companies disclose training data. The two subsequent lines each contain a subsidiary conclusion ('so claims remain unverifiable'; 'thus denying meaningful recourse'), and the final sentence provides a general supporting principle. All of these support the opening recommendation.
explanations.A: Intermediate-conclusion trap. The 'so' marker identifies this as a subsidiary conclusion supporting the main point, not the main point itself.
explanations.B: Correct. This paraphrases the opening sentence, which is the argument's core recommendation and the claim all subsequent statements are designed to support.
explanations.C: Intermediate-conclusion trap. The 'thus' marker identifies this as a subsidiary conclusion in the argument's second supporting strand; it supports the main recommendation but is not itself the main point.
explanations.D: Premise / supporting-principle trap. The final sentence is a general principle offered to reinforce the argument's recommendation, not the conclusion the argument is working toward.
explanations.E: Overstatement trap. The argument addresses the unverifiability of fairness claims and lack of individual recourse; it does not assert that biased training data inevitably produces unfair outcomes, nor does it use the word 'inevitably.'
